source_tasks.problem: The expression $4 \times  5 +  2 -  8 -  3 +  3 \times  5$ may be changed only by inserting parentheses; rearranging numbers or operations is not allowed. In total, how many values can be obtained?

Consider the expression $4 +  8 -  6 \cdot  6 -  4 +  2 \cdot  7$. Fully parenthesize it in every possible way without changing the order of numbers or operations. Parenthesizations with the same numerical result count only once. How many distinct values are possible?
The expression $7 +  6 \times  8 -  6 +  5 \times  3 -  5$ may be changed only by inserting parentheses; rearranging numbers or operations is not allowed. In total, how many values can be obtained?

observations: All three source questions ask for the number of distinct values obtainable by fully parenthesizing a fixed sequence of operands and binary operators (+,-,*) without reordering.
The shared interface supplies operands (integers) and operators (len(operands)-1 symbols from +,-,*), which exactly parameterizes the expression.
The requested quantity is the cardinality of the set of results over all full binary parenthesizations of the operator sequence.
This is a standard interval dynamic-programming problem: for each contiguous subexpression, compute the set of achievable values by splitting at each operator and combining left/right value sets.
Because operands are bounded (|value|<=10, length<=8) and only +,-,* are used, value sets stay small enough for exact set-based DP; no floating point is needed.
Duplicates must be collapsed per interval (sets), since the question counts distinct values only once.
analysis.procedure_plan: Implement solve(parameters): read operands a[0..n-1] and operators op[0..n-2]. If n==1 return 1 (single value). Build dp[i][j] = set of distinct integer values from fully parenthesizing a[i..j]. Initialize dp[i][i]={a[i]}. For length L from 2 to n, for each i, j=i+L-1, for each split k in [i, j-1]: combine every x in dp[i][k] with every y in dp[k+1][j] using op[k] (+,-,*), inserting results into dp[i][j]. Return the size of dp[0][n-1]. Use Python ints (arbitrary precision) to avoid overflow. Complexity O(n^3 * S^2) where S is max set size; fine for n<=8.
analysis.uncertainty: Set sizes could in principle grow, but with n<=8 and small operands the exact DP is tractable; worst-case set size is bounded by the number of parenthesizations (Catalan(7)=429) per interval, so combination work is modest. No ambiguity in the mathematical condition: full parenthesization preserving order, distinct values counted once.

source_tasks.problem: The expression $4 \times  5 +  2 -  8 -  3 +  3 \times  5$ may be changed only by inserting parentheses; rearranging numbers or operations is not allowed. In total, how many values can be obtained?

Consider the expression $4 +  8 -  6 \cdot  6 -  4 +  2 \cdot  7$. Fully parenthesize it in every possible way without changing the order of numbers or operations. Parenthesizations with the same numerical result count only once. How many distinct values are possible?
The expression $7 +  6 \times  8 -  6 +  5 \times  3 -  5$ may be changed only by inserting parentheses; rearranging numbers or operations is not allowed. In total, how many values can be obtained?

response.applicability: Valid for 1 to 8 integer operands each in [-10,20] and exactly len(operands)-1 operators drawn from '+','-','*'. Booleans are rejected as non-integers. Malformed inputs (wrong types, wrong operator count, out-of-range operands, unknown keys) raise ValueError. Returns the count of distinct values over all full parenthesizations preserving operand and operator order. Does not handle other operators, reordering, or larger operand counts.
response.description: Interval dynamic programming over the fixed operand/operator sequence. For each contiguous subexpression dp[i][j] we store the set of all distinct integer values reachable by fully parenthesizing operands i..j. Base case dp[i][i]={operands[i]}. For each length and split point k, combine every value from dp[i][k] with every value from dp[k+1][j] using operators[k], inserting into dp[i][j]. The answer is the cardinality of dp[0][n-1]. Sets collapse duplicates so each distinct value counts once. Python arbitrary-precision integers avoid overflow. Uncertainty: none in the mathematical condition; runtime is bounded because n<=8 and per-interval value sets are at most the number of parenthesizations (Catalan(7)=429), so the O(n^3 * S^2) combination is small.
